4Bad things can happen if or are not continuous

A function whose partial derivatives exist at the origin, yet the plane they produce is a terrible approximation there.

Bad things can happen if or are not continuous.

Example

Let

and exist (Ex. 54).

and , but neither nor is continuous. The tangent plane to at is the plane .

But at all points on the line (except ):

A last line starting “So …” was added at the bottom of this board after this photo was taken. Only the word “So” shows, at the right edge of Original images 10 and 11 (Section 7); no photo shows the rest of it, so it is not transcribed.

Explanation (added)

Why both partials are at the origin: on the x-axis for every , so ; the same on the y-axis gives . Putting these into the tangent-plane formula gives , the plane , which is what the board says.

But that plane does not approximate near the origin: at points of as close to as you like, . In fact is not even continuous at (approaching along gives , the two-path idea from 14.2). Stewart puts it this way: “the linear approximation would be , but at all points on the line ” (p. 977), and Exercise 54 asks you to show that is not differentiable at . So the plane comes out of the formula but is not a tangent plane in any useful sense, and that is the reason for the definition of “differentiable” in Section 7. “Ex. 54” on the board is Stewart §14.4, Exercise 54 (p. 983).

8The linear approximation, and a test for differentiability

(continuing from Section 7)

and underneath, in green (as are the labels , above):

Theorem

Theorem. If the partial derivatives and exist near , and are continuous at , then is differentiable at .

is continuous at means

Explanation (added)

The first line is the linear approximation (Stewart §14.4, Equation 4, p. 976). Moving to the left turns the left side into and the right side into ; the definition in Section 7 says these two differ only by .

The theorem is Stewart’s Theorem 8 (p. 977, proved in Appendix F). It is the test you actually use: checking Definition 7 directly is hard, but checking that and are continuous is usually quick, because polynomials, exponentials, sines and cosines, and quotients where the denominator is not are continuous, and so are their compositions (14.2). Section 4 shows why the word “continuous” is in the theorem: partial derivatives that merely exist are not enough.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Find the tangent plane or the linearization of at a point and use it to estimate a nearby value by hand, like in Section 3 (Stewart §14.4 Exercises 3–10 and 25).
  • “Explain why is differentiable at the point, then find ”: compute , , say why they are continuous there (Theorem 8), build , estimate a value (Exercises 15–22; Exercise 16 is the board’s ).
  • Find the differential (or for three variables) of a given function (Exercises 31–38).
  • Use differentials to estimate a change and a new value, as with in Section 12, or compare and (Exercises 39–40), or estimate the largest error (or the change) in a quantity computed from measurements (Exercises 41–50).
  • Theory: state the definition of differentiable or Theorem 8, or show that the partials of a function like the one in Section 4 exist at the origin but the function is not differentiable there (Exercises 53–54).
